English for University Studies and English for Working Abroad: ten
topics each, linked one by one from the 'I want to brush up my English'
routes on the home page (the #anchors must match the ids below).
Everything is written by RCF English. All names, emails, letters and
examples are invented. The working-abroad page gives language help only;
it is not legal, visa or employment advice.

pages.title: English for University Studies
pages.metaTitle: English for University Studies: Academic Vocabulary, Lectures, Reading, Referencing, Presentations | RCF English
pages.description: Brush up your English for university: academic vocabulary, assignment instruction words, taking notes in lectures, reading academic texts, paraphrasing and summarising, referencing, academic style, emails to lecturers, presentations and seminars.
pages.keywords: English for university students, academic English, academic vocabulary, note taking in lectures, paraphrasing, referencing and plagiarism, email to lecturer, academic presentation phrases, seminar discussion English

hero.text: University English is not harder English: it is English used for particular jobs, such as following a lecture, reading a research article or writing an assignment. Ten topics that make the first semester much easier.

blocks.heading: 1. Academic vocabulary
text: A small group of words appears again and again in lectures, textbooks and assignments, whatever your subject. Learn these first.

rows: facts that show something is true
There is little evidence for this claim.
large or important enough to notice
There was a significant increase in sales.
a way of dealing with something
This study uses a different approach.
one of the things that causes a result
a planned way of doing something
to accept something as true without proof
The model assumes that prices stay the same.
to decide after thinking about the evidence
The authors conclude that more research is needed.

blocks.heading: 2. Understanding assignment instructions
text: The first word of an assignment question tells you what to do. Students lose marks by describing when the question asks them to evaluate.

rows: Say what something is like, or what happened. No judgement is needed.
Say why or how something happens, with reasons.
Show the similarities and the differences.
Break a topic into parts and show how they are connected.
Look at different sides of an issue and reach a view.
Judge the strengths and weaknesses, and give a conclusion.
Give good reasons for a decision or opinion.
Give the main points only, briefly.

blocks.heading: 3. Following lectures and taking notes
text: You cannot write everything a lecturer says. Listen for the signpost phrases that show what is important, and use short forms to write faster.

parts.heading: Signposts to listen for
bullets: *The main point here is...* : write this down.
*There are three reasons...* : number your notes 1, 2, 3.
*For example...* : a short example helps you remember the idea.
*Moving on to...* : a new topic is starting.
*To sum up...* : the most important points are coming again.

blocks.heading: Short forms for faster notes
rows: is the same as / is different from

blocks.heading: 4. Reading academic texts efficiently
text: Academic texts are not read like novels, from the first word to the last. Read with a purpose, and decide quickly whether a text is useful.

parts.heading: A reading method
numbered: Before you read, write down what you want to find out.
Read the title, the abstract or introduction, and the conclusion first.
Look at the headings, tables and diagrams.
Now read the useful sections carefully, and make notes in your own words.
Write down the author, year and title straight away, for your references.

blocks.heading: 5. Paraphrasing and summarising
text: **Paraphrasing** means writing an idea in your own words and sentence structure. **Summarising** means giving only the main points, in fewer words. Both still need a reference to the original author.

parts.heading: How to paraphrase
numbered: Read the passage until you understand it fully.
Cover it, and write the idea from memory in your own words.
Compare with the original: change any phrases that are too close.

parts.heading: Example
text: **Original:** *Students who sleep for fewer than six hours a night tend to perform worse in examinations than those who sleep for eight hours.*
**Too close:** *Students who sleep fewer than six hours tend to do worse in exams than students sleeping eight hours.* (Only a few words have changed.)
**A good paraphrase:** *Getting too little sleep appears to be linked with lower examination results.* (Silva, 2022)
The example and the reference are invented for practice.

blocks.heading: 6. Referencing and avoiding plagiarism
text: **Plagiarism** is presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own, even by accident. Universities treat it very seriously. The solution is simple: whenever you use another person's idea, say where it came from.

parts.heading: The rules
bullets: Exact words go inside quotation marks, with a reference.
Paraphrased or summarised ideas also need a reference.
Common knowledge, such as *Colombo is the commercial capital of Sri Lanka*, needs no reference.
Every in-text reference must also appear in your reference list at the end.
Your university or department tells you which referencing style to use, such as APA or Harvard. Follow it exactly.

parts.heading: What an in-text reference often looks like
text: *Recent research suggests that group study improves memory (Fernando, 2021).*
The name and year are invented for this example. Check the exact format in your department's guide.

blocks.heading: 7. Writing in an academic style
text: Academic writing is formal, careful and precise. It avoids strong claims that cannot be proved.

rows: I think online learning is better.
Online learning may offer several advantages.

blocks.heading: 8. Emails to lecturers
text: A short, polite, clear email gets a faster reply. Use a clear subject line, a formal greeting, one purpose, and your name and course.

parts.heading: Example email
text: **Subject:** Question about Assignment 2 (BIO 101)
*Dear Dr Perera,*
*I am a first-year student in your Introduction to Biology course. I have a question about Assignment 2. The instructions ask for 1,500 words: does this include the reference list?*
*Thank you for your time.*
*Kind regards,*
*Tharushi Jayawardena*
*Student number: 2026/BIO/0123*
The names, course and number are invented for this example.

blocks.heading: 9. Giving a presentation
text: A good academic presentation tells the audience what is coming, delivers it clearly, and reminds them what they have heard.

rows: Good morning. Today I am going to talk about...
My presentation has three parts. First..., then..., and finally...
Now let us look at... / This brings me to my second point.
As you can see in this chart, ...
To sum up, ... / The key message is...
Thank you for listening. I would be happy to answer any questions.

blocks.heading: 10. Seminars and group discussions
text: In seminars you are expected to speak. You do not need a perfect idea: asking a good question or building on someone else's point also counts.

rows: In my view, ... / It seems to me that...
I agree with Nimal's point, because...
I see what you mean, but I wonder whether...
Building on that, ... / I would also add that...
Could you explain what you mean by...?

pages.title: English for Working Abroad
pages.metaTitle: English for Working Abroad: CV, Cover Letter, Job Interview, Workplace and Safety English | RCF English
pages.description: Brush up your English for a job overseas: writing a CV and cover letter, job interviews, your first days at work, understanding instructions and safety signs, telephone and email, serving customers, working with colleagues, and the words in a contract and payslip.
pages.keywords: English for foreign job, English for working abroad, English for migrant workers Sri Lanka, job interview English, CV in English, workplace English phrases, safety signs English, contract vocabulary

hero.text: Getting a job abroad starts with English, and keeping it depends on English too. Ten practical topics, from your CV to your first payslip.

blocks.title: About this page
text: This page helps with the English you need for work abroad. It is not legal, visa or employment advice. Before you accept a job or sign anything, check official guidance, for example from the Sri Lanka Bureau of Foreign Employment, and the rules of the country you are going to.

blocks.heading: 1. Writing a CV
text: A CV (curriculum vitae) is a short record of your experience and skills. Employers often look at it for less than a minute, so make it clear and easy to scan.

parts.heading: The usual sections
numbered: **Contact details:** name, phone number, email address.
**Personal profile:** two or three sentences about who you are and the job you want.
**Work experience:** most recent job first, with dates and what you did.
**Skills:** languages, computer skills, driving licence, and so on.

parts.heading: Tips
bullets: Start each duty with an action verb: *managed*, *prepared*, *repaired*, *served*, *trained*.
Keep it to one or two pages, and check every spelling.
CVs are different in different countries (for example, whether to include a photograph). Check what employers expect where you are applying.

parts.heading: Example lines
text: *Prepared meals for up to 200 guests a day in a busy hotel kitchen.*
*Maintained and repaired air-conditioning units in office buildings.*

blocks.heading: 2. Writing a cover letter or email
text: A cover letter introduces your CV. Keep it short: say which job you want, why you are suitable, and that you are available for an interview.

parts.heading: Example
text: *Dear Sir or Madam,*
*I am writing to apply for the position of Hotel Kitchen Assistant advertised on your website.*

*I have three years' experience in a busy hotel kitchen in Galle, where I prepared food, kept the kitchen clean and followed food safety rules. I work well in a team and I am used to working long shifts.*
*I have attached my CV, and I would welcome the opportunity to attend an interview.*
*Yours faithfully,*
*Chaminda Rathnayake*
The name and details are invented for this example.

blocks.heading: 3. The job interview
text: Most interviews use similar questions. Prepare an answer to each, and practise saying it aloud, not just reading it.

rows: Your experience and skills in two or three sentences, linked to this job.
Why do you want this job?
What interests you about the work, not only the salary.
One or two real examples of what you did.
A strength with a short example that proves it.
Tell me about a problem you solved at work.
The situation, what you did, and the result.
Always ask one: for example, about training or working hours.

blocks.title: Practise out loud
text: The [Conversation Partner](practical-english/conversation-partner/) has a job interview you can answer with your voice, and [Speaking Practice](speaking-practice/?mode=talk) lets you practise introducing yourself.

blocks.heading: 4. Your first days at work
text: In the first week, people will not expect you to know everything, but they will expect you to ask.

rows: Hello, I'm Kamal. I've just started in the stores department.
What time do I start and finish?
Where should I put my things?
Who should I ask if I have a problem?
Could you show me how this works, please?

blocks.heading: 5. Understanding and checking instructions
text: Doing a task wrongly because you were too shy to ask can cost money or cause accidents. Always check instructions you are not sure about. Repeating them back is the best way.

rows: Sorry, could you say that again more slowly?
Just to check: you want me to clean the rooms on floor two first?
What does *urgent* mean here? Today, or right now?
Could you write that down for me, please?

blocks.heading: 6. Safety signs and warnings
text: Safety signs use short words that you must understand immediately. Learn these before your first day.

rows: Serious risk of injury or death
Be careful: there is a risk
Do not go in unless you have permission
The way out in an emergency
Wear the gloves, helmet, glasses or boots provided
Where to find help and medical supplies

blocks.title: Report a problem at once
text: If something is unsafe, say so immediately: *Excuse me, this machine isn't working properly. I think it's dangerous.* You are never wrong to report a safety problem.

blocks.heading: 7. Telephone calls and work messages
text: When you are ill or late, tell your supervisor as early as possible, clearly and politely.

parts.heading: Calling in sick
text: *Good morning, this is Sunil from the night shift. I'm sorry, but I'm ill today and I can't come to work. I'll let you know how I am tomorrow.*

parts.heading: A short message about being late
text: *Hello Ms Lee, my bus has broken down. I'm sorry, I will be about 30 minutes late. Sunil*
The names are invented for these examples.

blocks.heading: 8. Serving customers and handling complaints
text: In hotels, shops, restaurants and care work, your English is part of the service. When a customer complains, follow four steps: **listen, apologise, solve, thank.**

rows: Good afternoon. How can I help you?
I understand. Could you tell me exactly what happened?
Let me fix that for you right away. / I'll ask my manager.
Thank you for letting us know.

blocks.heading: 9. Working with colleagues
text: Friendly, polite English makes working together easier, especially in teams where people come from many countries.

rows: Could you give me a hand with this?
No problem, I'll do it now.
Sorry, I can't right now. I'm finishing this job.
Would it be possible to take Friday off?

blocks.heading: 10. Words in your contract and payslip
text: Never sign a contract you do not fully understand. Ask for a copy, take your time, and ask someone you trust to read it with you.

rows: the money you are paid, often monthly (salary) or hourly (wage)
your pay before extra money is added
extra hours worked beyond your normal hours
a set period of work, such as a night shift
money taken from your pay, for example for tax or accommodation
the first weeks or months, when your work is checked
how long before leaving you must tell your employer
